methods.name: Peer-Median
methods.skip_reason: insufficient narrow peer set in Drones & Autonomous (found 0 same-stage, 0 adjacent-stage, 0 similar-tier; need ≥3)
methods.rationale: 5 same-sector peers exist in Drones & Autonomous, but none of the narrow filters (same-stage / adjacent-stage / similar-valuation-tier) yielded ≥3 datapoints. Falling back to all-sector median would be misleading.

data.narrative:
ACSL, a publicly listed drone and autonomous systems company trading on the Tokyo exchange, presents a valuation challenge due to the nascent state of its peer universe. The Drones & Autonomous sector contains only six identified private comparables—Zipline, Joby Aviation, Nuro, Archer Aviation, and Elroy Air among them—with zero public peers and no same-stage or adjacent-stage companies meeting minimum clustering thresholds. This fragmentation prevents application of traditional peer-median methodologies, which require at least three comparable datapoints within defined stage and valuation bands.

Given the absence of a sufficiently granular peer set, conventional triangulation methods prove inapplicable to this analysis. The sector lacks public trading comps entirely, and the private comparables span divergent applications (last-mile delivery, urban air mobility, autonomous ground vehicles) and financing stages, making normalized revenue or EBITDA multiples unreliable. A peer-median approach using all-sector data would introduce unacceptable noise and misrepresent ACSL's specific risk and growth profile.

Without sufficient homogeneous comparables, a credible valuation range cannot be derived from standard market-based approaches. Alternative methods—such as discounted cash flow analysis using ACSL-specific assumptions or precedent transaction analysis within autonomous systems—would be required to establish a defensible valuation. The core uncertainty remains the structural immaturity of the Drones & Autonomous public and private markets.
